lines: Here are 3 postpartum fitness myths you need to stop believing.
The first myth is that walking alone is enough to recover. Walking is wonderful for fresh air, but it does not rebuild your deep core or pelvic floor.
The second myth is doing standard crunches to fix your belly. Crunches push outward on healing tissue, which makes diastasis recti worse instead of knitting it back together.

The third myth is thinking you need gentle hour long sessions. You do not need an hour you will skip. Thirty smart, focused minutes of controlled strength training beats endless light cardio every time.
Training postpartum is not about bouncing back quickly. It is about building functional strength so you can carry your toddler up the stairs without stopping.
Save this video for your next home session, and comment below which myth you believed.

lines: Most market shoppers walk past because your table is flat.

When someone is walking down a crowded vendor aisle, their eyes scan naturally at eye level and chest height. If everything you make is resting flat on a tablecloth, they have to physically stop, tilt their head down, and work to see your inventory.

Shoppers avoid awkward friction. If scanning your booth feels like effort, they will keep walking to the next tent without even realizing why. You have less than three seconds to catch their peripheral vision before they step past your space.
The fix is not cramming more products onto the table. That only makes the space feel messy and overwhelming to look at.

Instead, build three clear height zones. Place your tallest risers in the back corners, medium tiers in the middle center, and keep the front edge open for clean spacing. This creates an automatic visual staircase that pulls the eye directly across your entire collection.
When your display meets customers at their natural line of sight, browsing feels effortless, and people stop without even planning to.

lines: I'm going to do a little bit of the same thing right in the center so your loaf stops spreading flat.

Most people think flat loaves happen because you lack a commercial proofer, but it usually comes down to how you handle tension during the initial pre-shape. When you drag the outer skin across the board without securing the middle, the whole structure collapses as soon as it heats up.

If you only pull the outside edges, you create a thin skin that tears in the oven. What you actually want is internal resistance, where the core of the dough pushes back against your hands while the seam stays tight underneath.

Here is the exact fix: take the top third, fold it down, and press right in the middle to create an anchor point. Then roll the sides gently over that center lock so the whole ball tightens naturally without tearing the surface.
Once that center seam is locked, your loaf holds a clean dome shape and rises straight up in any standard home oven. That is the entire routine, and I will see you in the next video.

lines: I feel like nobody talks about how total rest ruins knee recovery.

I am a sports physiotherapist, and I completely understand why you want to keep the leg still when it hurts. You are trying to protect the joint from further damage, which feels like the safest decision.

The problem is that total immobilization causes rapid quadriceps inhibition and joint stiffness. When swelling sits inside the capsule without gentle muscle contraction, your brain literally shuts off full communication with your thigh.

This is where people get stuck for months. If you lose passive knee extension in the first couple of weeks, restoring a normal walking gait becomes significantly harder and delays your return to sport.

The easiest way to prevent this is introducing early quad sets and passive extension immediately. Even sitting on a chair and gently sliding your heel along a laminate floor keeps the joint moving without overloading healing tissue.

lines: I am going to show you how to price your sourdough loaves. When you launch a home microbakery, figuring out what to charge can feel intimidating, but the basic math is very straightforward.

First, calculate the raw ingredient cost for a single standard loaf. Measure out your flour, filtered water, salt, and sourdough starter. In a typical home batch, those four ingredients usually add up to about one dollar and fifty cents total.

Next, factor in the packaging expenses that most beginners completely overlook. Your kraft bread bag, custom label sticker, and parchment paper usually add another fifty to seventy five cents per loaf, bringing your true base cost to roughly two dollars and twenty five cents.
Now apply the simple three times rule to build your price. One third covers your direct unit costs, one third handles cottage kitchen overhead and utilities, and one third pays your labor and profit.
Multiplying your two dollar base cost by three gives you an absolute minimum of seven dollars, which positions a standard artisan loaf perfectly at nine to ten dollars for local pickup orders.
That simple formula keeps your microbakery sustainable right from your home kitchen. Let me know in the comments what you currently charge for your loaves, and I will see you in the next video.
